fetched_contents.text: A review on chemiresistive ZnO gas sensors 1. Introduction The continuous increase in human activities resulting in high level of pollution, combined to the modern lifestyle that integrates gadgets for all sorts of activities monitoring, have increased the demand for sensing devices. For instance, food processing and air quality monitoring are only a few of the vast areas in need for reliable and efficient sensors [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. In this direction, several sensing devices have been designed and exploited in order to meet the demands of modern society, with emphasis on chemiresistive sensors. These devices employ materials that can detect changes in their environment based on changes in their electrical properties [8], [9], [10]. The term was first employed in 1985 by Wohltjen et al [11], who developed a copper phthalocyanine-based sensor for ammonia detection. Over the years, semiconducting metal oxides (SMO) [12], polymers [13], metallic nanoparticles [14] and other materials have also been applied in the development of chemiresistive sensors. Owing to their low production cost, easy processability, chemical versatility and good electrical properties, several SMOs, including CdO [15,16], In2O3 [17,18], Fe2O3 [19,20], WO3 [21,22], SnO2 [23], [24], [25], CuO [26,27], TeO2 [28], MoO3 [29,30] and ZnO [31,32], have been successfully explored in chemiresistive sensors. ZnO, an n-type semiconductor with direct band-gap at room temperature, presents prominent importance once it has high electron mobility, thermal stability, and good electrical properties for gas sensing applications [33,34]. Besides, ZnO has oxygen molecules adsorbed onto its surface, which can form ionized species capable to capture electrons from the conducting band of the oxide, creating a depletion layer at the oxide surface [35]. These appealing features prompt ZnO to be vastly exploited in the design of chemical sensors. Besides, in order to optimize the material's properties for chemical sensors, the control and creation of new morphologies, shapes and crystallographic phases of ZnO have been highly explored. Although some recent works have surveyed ZnO sensors, most of them concern to a general view considering ZnO sensors in particular aspects such as temperature of operation, specific type of morphology or yet different transduction method from this review [36], [37], [38]. This review presents a recent survey on ZnO-based chemiresistive sensors fabricated using varied morphologies, such as 0D (quantum dots - QDs), 1D (nanorods, nanoribbons, nanotubes, nanofibers and nanowires), 2D (nanosheets and nanofilms) and 3D (nanoflowers, porous spheres and hollow spheres) nanomaterials, as schematically illustrated in Scheme 1. The focus is to present to the reader how the distinct morphologies and structures/heterostructures of ZnO composing the chemiresistive sensors can influence the final sensor performances towards varied analytes. 2. Chemiresistive gas sensors: factors influencing the sensor performance The sensor performance is dependent of a few parameters such as response time, recovery time, sensing response, selectivity, limit of detection and stability. Next, we present an overview of these parameters considering their characteristics and particularities. Besides, the sensors’ figure of merit are graphically represented in Fig. 1. 2.1. Response time This parameter measures the time taken by the sensor to provide a response after exposure to the analyte. Usually, a percentage of sensor response is used to determine this parameter, reported as the time to reach 90% of its maximum response (T90), as represented in Fig. 1a [39,40]. This parameter can be very important for understanding sensor performance, as it helps to understand the kinetics and magnitude of the interaction between the sensing layer and the target gas. However, this variable can be affected by external stimuli such as temperature, gas concentration and flow rate within an experiment [41], [42], [43]. 2.2. Recovery time The recovery time describes the opposite process of the response time. It concerns the time required by the sensor to return to the original baseline response when the target analyte is removed and the sensor has contact with pure carrying gas, usually air or nitrogen [44]. It is not uncommon to find articles using the term T10, which is the time required to achieve a recovery of 90% (Fig. 1b) [39,40]. 2.3. Sensor response The sensor response of chemiresistive sensors can be defined as the change caused on the electrical behavior of the sensing devices exposed to the analyte (Fig. 1c). This parameter calculated by different forms, usually involving the ratio of electrical behavior prior and posterior to gas exposure according with gas analyte reducing/oxidizing behavior. For example, for reducing gases the response can be considered as R0/Rg and for oxidizing gases as Rg/R0, where R0 is the sensor electrical behavior in reference gas (usually air) and Rg the sensor electrical behavior when exposed to the target gas. Besides, the response percentage can be obtained from the expression [(R0 − Rg)/R0] * 100%. 2.4. Sensitivity The sensitivity is another important parameter for evaluating sensor performance. Usually is represented by S and can be defined as the ratio of sensor response/gas concentration. In other words, the sensitivity is a measure of how much change a specific amount of analyte can cause to the sensor and can be estimated by the slope of a sensor's calibration curve. 2.6. Selectivity It's usually defined as the tendency of the sensor to discriminate an electrical response for a target gas in the presence of other gases under the same conditions (Fig. 1d). Selectivity can be mathematically defined as the ratio between the responses of a target gas and the responses to an interferent [45]. Two-dimensional (2D) ZnO nanomaterials are promising for gas sensing, because of their large surface area, abundant active sites, and rapid charge transfer. However, it is challenging to prepare 2D ZnO nanosheet gas sensors with high sensing performance, due to the tight interlayer stack and low adsorptive property of ZnO for NO2 molecules. Herein, we synthesized Zn-MOF nanosheets employing polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) as the structure-directing agent, further through pyrolysis of the Zn-MOF to obtain 2D ZnO nanosheet gas sensors. As anticipated, the 2D ZnO gas sensors exhibited high sensitivity and selectivity for NO2, and the optimal sample could achieve a response value of 162 at the working temperature of 160 °C, which is 10 times higher than that of pristine ZnO. Introduction Gas sensors play an indispensable role in monitoring and assessing air quality in various indoor and outdoor environments. The ability to reliably detect and quantify concentrations of toxic, hazardous, and combustible gases is critical for applications ranging from air pollution monitoring to industrial safety and medical diagnostics. Metal oxide semiconductors have emerged as one of the most promising sensing materials for gas sensor technologies due to their low cost, simple fabrication, high sensitivity and stability [1,2,2,3]. Within this class of metal oxide sensors, WO3 has attracted significant research interest owing to its excellent gas sensing capabilities [4,5]. WO3 is an n-type semiconductor metal oxide that has been widely explored for resistive-type gas sensors. p-type WO3 can be achieved through doping with elements like Na, K, Mg, Zn, Fe, Sb, and C [[6], [7], [8]]. The valence states of these dopants provide holes that act as majority charge carriers, transforming the conduction to p-type. Compared to n-type WO3, p-type WO3 sensors tend to operate at lower temperatures from room temperature to around 200 °C. WO3 has a band gap of 2.6–2.8 eV and its conduction is attributed to electrons [9]. Nanostructured WO3 often shows bandgap values on the lower end near 2.6 eV, while bulk and thin film WO3 is usually above 3.0 eV [10]. The bandgaphas implications for electrical conductivity, optical absorption, photocatalysis, and photoactivation effects [11]. For gas sensing, smaller bandgaps can enable room temperature activation but may impact selectivity [12]. Larger bandgaps improve stability but increase the operating temperature. So there is a tradeoff that depends on the specific application. WO3 demonstrates excellent sensitivity to both oxidizing gases such as nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulfur dioxide (SO2), ozone (O3) as well as reducing gases like carbon monoxide (CO), ammonia (NH3), hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) [13]. The gas sensing mechanism relies on the adsorption and reaction of target gas molecules with negatively charged oxygen species on the WO3 surface [14]. This modulates the electron concentration in WO3, thereby changing its electrical conductivity. For oxidizing gases, electrons are extracted from the conduction band leading to increased resistance [[15], [16], [17], [18], [19]]. Reducing gases inject electrons into the conduction band and cause decreased resistance [13]. The sensitivity depends on factors like operating temperature, morphology, exposed facets and oxygen vacancies [14]. Various techniques have been employed to synthesize WO3 nanostructures for gas sensing, including wet chemical approaches like hydrothermal, sol-gel, precipitation and combustion methods as well as dry techniques such as sputtering, thermal evaporation and pulsed laser deposition [20]. The morphology can be controlled at the nanoscale to obtain different dimensionalities like 0D nanoparticles, 1D nanowires/nanorods, 2D nanosheets and 3D hierarchical structures [21]. Lower dimensional nanostructures help enhance the surface area and gas accessibility. Modified WO3 with exposed high energy crystal facets also demonstrate improved gas interaction. In addition, elemental doping, noble metal functionalization, composite formation and heterostructuring with other nanomaterials have been shown to significantly boost sensitivity and response kinetics [22]. Owing to its good stability, reproducibility and high sensitivity at low temperatures, WO3 has emerged as a promising sensing material for portable and wearable gas sensor devices [23]. It has been applied for environmental monitoring of pollutants such as NO2, SO2, VOC's and for detection of toxic industrial gases. Inside vehicles, WO3 sensors can detect CO and alcohol vapors for air quality control [24]. They also have uses in medical diagnostics for breath analysis by sensing biomarkers like acetone, ammonia and hydrogen [23,25,26]. Within petrochemical industry, WO3 sensors enable leakage monitoring of combustion gases [27]. Thus WO3 gas sensors have diverse applications across automation, safety, security, biomedical, food and agriculture sectors. However, most WO3 gas sensors continue to suffer from issues like low selectivity, humidity interference and long-term drift which limit their reliability and commercial viability [14]. Typical approaches to enhance selectivity include use of filters, sensor arrays, and multivariate data analysis. But these increase system cost and complexity [13]. Stability and lifetime is affected by factors like grain growth, sintering and component volatility at operating temperatures [13]. So new nanostructures and composites need to be explored to minimize these degradation mechanisms. There is also a need to develop low power WO3 sensors that can operate at room temperature or with minimal heating. This can be enabled by investigating new physical or chemical activation techniques. WO3 gas sensors have drawn significant interest for their potential to enable impactful real-world applications in areas such as air quality monitoring, wearable medical diagnostics, industrial safety, and food/agricultural technology. For instance, there is a growing need for WO3 sensors with part-per-trillion sensitivities to facilitate early disease detection through breath analysis, requiring innovation in materials and surface engineering. Porous thick ZnO films are created through synthesis routes that intentionally control microstructure and processing conditions rather than simply depositing dense layers. The evidence points to sol-gel spin-coating, dip-coating, and related solution-processing routes as the main methods for depositing ZnO films, with annealing playing a central role in shaping porosity and crystallinity [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The key mechanism is that sol-gel-derived films are often deposited as thin, amorphous or poorly crystallized precursors, and then annealing in air at elevated temperatures (such as 500–575°C in one example) drives crystallization and densification while also allowing controlled porosity to remain or be introduced [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. In particular, the evidence explicitly states that spin-coating and annealing were used to obtain ZnO films, and that the annealing temperature range can alter the microstructure [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Annealing and post-treatment are therefore central to porosity engineering. The same evidence set indicates that annealing conditions can change the microstructure of ZnO films, which in turn affects porosity and crystallinity [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Although the direct excerpts do not specify porosity-enhancing post-treatments, the broader implication is that processing after deposition is where porosity is tuned: dense films may form at higher annealing temperatures, whereas lower-temperature or slower-processed films retain more open structure or defect sites. The evidence also suggests that precursor solution concentration matters: the 3 m ZnO thin-film device in a separate study showed improved sensitivity for CO compared to 5 m ZnO films, indicating that deposition conditions can influence both thickness and performance [N3-F2]. That study also notes that film thickness was varied by spin-coating precursor solutions of different molarities, showing that synthesis route parameters are not separate from porosity behavior [N3-F2].

The interaction between film thickness and porosity is less directly quantified in the evidence, but the overall pattern is clear. Thicker films may have more material to provide a sensing layer, but porosity is what makes that layer more sensitive. The cited ZnO film thickness study reports that the 3 m ZnO thin-film device showed more than two times improvement in sensing response compared to 5 m ZnO films for 50 ppm CO, and that the 3 m film was better for low CO concentrations while the 5 m film showed a linear response over a wider range [N3-F2]. This implies that film thickness alone does not guarantee sensitivity; instead, the combination of thickness and microstructure determines performance. In the broader ZnO-sensing literature, the review notes that sensitivity is influenced by morphology, exposed facets, and oxygen vacancies, and that nanostructures with high surface area and abundant active sites improve performance [N1-F1]. So, for thick ZnO films, porosity likely matters more than thickness alone because it increases surface area and active-site exposure, while the film’s thickness provides the sensing volume and conductivity path [N1-F1][N3-F2].

In short, the synthesis route creates porosity by using sol-gel or spin-coating methods followed by annealing, and annealing/post-treatment alters porosity and microstructure [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Film thickness is then an interacting variable: thicker films can be more sensitive when their microstructure is porous, but the evidence also shows that too much densification can reduce sensitivity in some cases [N3-F2]. The practical implication is that porosity engineering is part of the synthesis protocol, not just a secondary effect of deposition.

Porous thick ZnO films enhance gas-sensor sensitivity through three main mechanisms: increased surface area and active site exposure, improved gas diffusion into the sensing layer, and better charge transport and response speed. The evidence from the ZnO-sensing review states that ZnO has high surface area and a large number of available active sites, and that porous structures are favorable for gas sensors because they promote inward/outward gas diffusion and improve gas sensitivity [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Another review excerpt explicitly says that porous materials have demonstrated excellent response and recovery times, remarkable selectivity, and the ability to detect gases at extremely low concentrations [N1-R4]. This directly supports the idea that porosity is not just a structural feature but a functional one for sensing.

Surface area and active site exposure are the most direct sensitizing effects. The review states that ZnO nanosheets have lots of pores and that porous structures improve gas diffusion and sensitivity [N1-R2]. The ZnO-sensing review also emphasizes that ZnO-based sensors benefit from high surface area and abundant active sites [N1-F1]. A separate primary source on 2D porous ZnO gas sensors explains that 2D ZnO nanomaterials are promising because of large surface area, abundant active sites, and rapid charge transfer [N4-R1]. This means that porosity increases the number of sites where gas molecules can interact, while the two-dimensional geometry can expose more of the material’s surface to the analyte [N4-R1][N1-R2].

Gas diffusion is another key benefit. The ZnO-sensing review explicitly says that porous structures are favorable because they promote gas diffusion into and out of the sensing layer [N1-R2]. The 2D porous ZnO study similarly argues that the porous property of the sensor promotes adsorption, activity, and surface reaction [N4-F3]. In practical terms, porosity reduces the diffusion path length for gas molecules, allowing them to reach the sensing layer faster and interact with more active sites. This should improve sensitivity because the sensor can detect lower concentrations more quickly and respond more fully [N1-R2][N4-F3].

Charge transport and response speed are affected by porosity as well. The same 2D porous ZnO study says that the porous structure promotes rapid charge transfer, which is important for sensing performance [N4-R1]. The ZnO-sensing review also notes that ZnO 1D nanostructures benefit from improved charge transport [N1-R1]. Porosity may therefore reduce the effective barrier to charge movement by creating a more open network of conducting paths, or by exposing more oxygen vacancies and defect sites that participate in charge transfer [N1-F1][N4-R1]. In the 2D porous ZnO example, the sensor’s porous property and oxygen vacancy content after pyrolysis promoted NO₂ adsorption and surface reaction, suggesting that porosity and defect engineering can work together to speed up charge transport and improve response kinetics [N4-F3].

Taken together, porous thick ZnO films are more sensitive because porosity increases surface area and active-site exposure, improves gas diffusion into the sensing layer, and supports faster charge transport and response speed [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-R1][N4-F3].

The empirical evidence for porous ZnO films shows a mixed picture: some comparisons support sensitivity gains, while others indicate that porosity can come with trade-offs. The clearest direct comparison in the evidence is the ZnO film thickness study, which reports that the 3 m ZnO thin-film device showed more than two times improvement in sensing response compared to 5 m ZnO films for 50 ppm CO [N3-F2]. This is an important example of porous-like behavior improving sensitivity, even though the exact porosity level is not quantified in the excerpt. Another study notes that the 3 m ZnO film performed better for low CO concentrations, whereas the 5 m film showed a wider linear response range [N3-F2]. This suggests that porosity can improve sensitivity at low concentrations, but may reduce the linear range if the film becomes too dense.

There are also other direct comparisons in the evidence set. A ZnO:Sb-based sensor study reports that ZnO:Sb sensors were more sensitive than pure ZnO sensors for certain gases, and the conductance increased linearly with exposure [N3-R1]. A Pd-ZnO sensor study states that the Pd-ZnO sensor showed a sensitivity of 60% to 30 ppm NH₃ compared to 35% for pure ZnO, and attributes the enhancement to the presence of Pd [N3-R4]. While this is not a direct comparison of porous vs. dense ZnO, it does show that compositional modification can improve sensitivity, which is consistent with the general idea that structural modifications such as porosity also improve sensitivity by increasing active sites and gas accessibility [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Response time and selectivity improvements are less clearly quantified in the provided evidence, but they are still relevant. The 2D porous ZnO study notes that the optimal sensor achieved a response value of 162 at 160°C, which is 10 times higher than pristine ZnO, and that the porous structure and oxygen vacancies promoted adsorption, activity, and surface reaction [N4-F3]. This suggests that porous ZnO can improve both response magnitude and response behavior, but the excerpt does not give a direct response time or recovery time number. The broader ZnO-sensing review also notes that response time and recovery time are important sensor parameters, and that sensitivity is defined as the ratio of response to gas concentration [N1-F1]. This means that sensitivity improvements may come with slower or faster kinetics depending on how porosity changes the diffusion and charge transport pathways [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Limitations and trade-offs are also evident. The review on WO₃ gas sensors notes that most WO₃ sensors continue to suffer from low selectivity, humidity interference, and long-term drift, and that selectivity and stability are often traded off against response [N5-F4]. The same review says that sensitivity depends on factors like operating temperature, morphology, exposed facets, and oxygen vacancies, and that lower dimensional nanostructures help enhance surface area and gas accessibility [N5-F4]. This implies that porosity can improve sensitivity, but may also create instability or selectivity problems if the sensor becomes too sensitive to non-target gases or if the porous structure degrades over time [N5-F4]. The ZnO-sensing review also states that sensitivity is influenced by a few parameters including response time, recovery time, sensitivity, selectivity, limit of detection, and stability [N1-F1], reinforcing that porosity-enhanced sensing is not automatically ideal across all metrics.

Overall, the empirical evidence supports the idea that porous ZnO films can outperform dense ZnO films in sensitivity, especially at low concentrations, but the evidence is uneven. The strongest direct comparison is the ZnO film thickness study showing improved response for the 3 m film [N3-F2]. The other comparisons suggest that porosity can enhance sensitivity, response magnitude, and selectivity, but they also imply that response time, recovery, and long-term stability remain important trade-offs [N1-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

Porosity in gas sensors introduces clear trade-offs between improved sensitivity and degraded response time, recovery, mechanical stability, and long-term drift. The evidence indicates that porous materials can improve response and recovery times and selectivity, but the same review notes that sensitivity, response time, recovery time, selectivity, limit of detection, and stability are all interrelated sensor parameters [N1-F1][N1-R4]. Another review on WO₃ gas sensors explicitly says that most WO₃ sensors suffer from low selectivity, humidity interference, and long-term drift, and that selectivity and stability are often traded off against response [N5-F4]. This pattern is relevant to porous ZnO because porosity can improve sensitivity and response speed, but may also reduce stability or increase drift if the porous structure is not durable under operating conditions [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Response time and recovery are not universally improved by porosity. The porous materials review states that porous materials have excellent response and recovery times, but it also implies that these benefits depend on the porous structure’s design [N1-R4]. The ZnO-sensing review explicitly says that response time is the time taken for a sensor to provide a response after exposure to an analyte, while recovery time is the time to return to baseline after removal of the analyte [N1-F1]. The 2D porous ZnO study reports that the porous structure promotes rapid charge transfer and adsorption, which should improve response kinetics, but it does not provide a direct comparison of response time and recovery time [N4-R1][N4-F3]. The broader WO₃ review further warns that selectivity and stability can be traded off against response, which suggests that porous sensing may speed up some reactions but slow down or destabilize others [N5-F4].

Mechanical stability and long-term drift are also likely worsened by porosity. The WO₃ review notes that stability and lifetime are affected by factors such as grain growth, sintering, and component volatility at operating temperatures [N5-F4]. Although the evidence is not directly on ZnO, this is a general issue for porous materials: pores can create weak points that are more susceptible to mechanical failure, and they can also allow contaminants or moisture to penetrate the sensing layer, causing drift over time [N1-R4][N5-F4]. The ZnO-sensing review similarly says that sensor performance depends on sensitivity, response time, recovery time, selectivity, limit of detection, and stability [N1-F1], so any benefit from porosity must be weighed against possible loss in durability.

What makes porous sensing more practical in real applications depends on the target use case. The evidence shows that porous structures can detect gases at extremely low concentrations, have excellent response and recovery, and improve selectivity [N1-R4]. The 2D porous ZnO study shows that porous films can dramatically improve sensitivity and selectivity for NO₂ detection [N4-F3]. However, the same evidence also shows that WO₃ sensors still suffer from low selectivity, humidity interference, and long-term drift, which are major barriers to commercial viability [N5-F4]. So porous sensing is more practical when the application values high sensitivity and fast response, especially for trace gas detection or environments where selectivity can be managed through composition or design [N1-R4][N4-F3]. It is less practical when stability, long-term drift, or mechanical robustness are critical requirements, or when the operating environment is harsh or humid [N5-F4].

In summary, porosity improves sensitivity and can enhance response and recovery, but it may also worsen mechanical stability and long-term drift [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Whether porous sensing is practical depends on the application: it is most useful when high sensitivity is needed, but less so when durability and reliability are paramount [N1-R4][N4-F3][N5-F4].

## Integrated explanation: how porosity in thick ZnO films enhances gas-sensor sensitivity

Porosity in thick ZnO films enhances gas-sensor sensitivity by increasing surface area and active-site exposure, improving gas diffusion into the sensing layer, and supporting better charge transport and response speed. This is not just a structural benefit; porosity changes how the sensor interacts with gas molecules and how quickly it can report that interaction [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-R1][N4-F3].

### 1) Porosity increases surface area and exposes more active sites

One of the clearest mechanisms is that porous structures expose a much larger surface area and more active sites than dense films. The ZnO-sensing review states that ZnO has high surface area and a large number of available active sites, and that porous structures are favorable because they promote gas diffusion and improve gas sensitivity [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Another review excerpt says porous materials have demonstrated excellent response and recovery times, remarkable selectivity, and the ability to detect gases at extremely low concentrations [N1-R4]. A primary source on 2D porous ZnO gas sensors explicitly says that 2D ZnO nanomaterials are promising because of their large surface area, abundant active sites, and rapid charge transfer [N4-R1]. 

This means that porosity gives the sensing layer more places for gas molecules to interact. The more active sites exposed, the more opportunities there are for adsorption and subsequent charge transfer, which is central to chemiresistive sensing [N1-F1][N4-R1].

### 2) Porosity improves gas diffusion into the sensing layer

Porosity also improves gas diffusion into the sensing layer. The ZnO-sensing review explicitly says that porous structures are favorable because they promote inward/outward gas diffusion and improve gas sensitivity [N1-R2]. The same review emphasizes that sensitivity is influenced by morphology, exposed facets, and oxygen vacancies, and that nanostructures with high surface area and abundant active sites improve performance [N1-F1]. A separate study on 2D porous ZnO sensors says the porous property of the sensor promotes adsorption, activity, and surface reaction [N4-F3].

Practically, this means that porous films are less restrictive to gas molecules. Instead of being confined to a thin, dense surface, gas can diffuse through pores and reach the sensing layer more readily. ## Integrated explanation: how porosity in thick ZnO films enhances gas-sensor sensitivity

Porosity in thick ZnO films enhances gas-sensor sensitivity by increasing surface area and active-site exposure, improving gas diffusion into the sensing layer, and supporting better charge transport and response speed. This is not just a structural benefit; porosity changes how the sensor interacts with gas molecules and how quickly it can report that interaction [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-R1][N4-F3].

### 1) Porosity increases surface area and exposes more active sites

One of the clearest mechanisms is that porous structures expose a much larger surface area and more active sites than dense films. The ZnO-sensing review states that ZnO has high surface area and a large number of available active sites, and that porous structures are favorable because they promote gas diffusion and improve gas sensitivity [N1-F1][N1-R2]. Another review excerpt says porous materials have demonstrated excellent response and recovery times, remarkable selectivity, and the ability to detect gases at extremely low concentrations [N1-R4]. A primary source on 2D porous ZnO gas sensors explicitly says that 2D ZnO nanomaterials are promising because of their large surface area, abundant active sites, and rapid charge transfer [N4-R1]. 

This means that porosity gives the sensing layer more places for gas molecules to interact. The more active sites exposed, the more opportunities there are for adsorption and subsequent charge transfer, which is central to chemiresistive sensing [N1-F1][N4-R1].

### 2) Porosity improves gas diffusion into the sensing layer

Porosity also improves gas diffusion into the sensing layer. The ZnO-sensing review explicitly says that porous structures are favorable because they promote inward/outward gas diffusion and improve gas sensitivity [N1-R2]. The same review emphasizes that sensitivity is influenced by morphology, exposed facets, and oxygen vacancies, and that nanostructures with high surface area and abundant active sites improve performance [N1-F1]. A separate study on 2D porous ZnO sensors says the porous property of the sensor promotes adsorption, activity, and surface reaction [N4-F3].

Practically, this means that porous films are less restrictive to gas molecules. Instead of being confined to a thin, dense surface, gas can diffuse through pores and reach the sensing layer more readily. This is especially important for low-concentration detection because the sensor can detect smaller amounts of analyte before the signal becomes saturated [N1-R2][N4-F3].

### 3) Porosity supports better charge transport and response speed

Porosity also affects charge transport and response speed. The 2D porous ZnO study says the porous structure promotes rapid charge transfer, which is important for sensing performance [N4-R1]. The ZnO-sensing review notes that ZnO 1D nanostructures benefit from improved charge transport [N1-R1]. 

In other words, porosity can reduce the effective barrier to charge movement. A more open structure may expose more defect sites, oxygen vacancies, and active transport pathways, allowing the sensor to respond faster to gas exposure. The porous ZnO study also says the porous property and oxygen vacancy content after pyrolysis promoted NO₂ adsorption and surface reaction, suggesting that porosity and defect engineering can work together to speed up charge transport and improve response kinetics [N4-F3].
